items.stem: In a Philippine province with coastal mangroves there were 300 km² of forest, and 2% of the remaining forest is being lost each year. (a) Calculate the forest area remaining after 5 years. (b) Calculate how long it would take to lose half the forest at this rate. (c) Explain two reasons why biodiversity loss may be greater than the percentage of area lost suggests.
items.answer: (a) 300 × (1 − 0.02)^5 ≈ 271 km² (b) ln 0.5 / ln(1 − 0.02) ≈ 34 years (c) fragmentation increases edge effects and isolates populations (small populations, inbreeding); loss is concentrated in lowland, species-rich areas; species–area relationship and extinction debt; roads open remaining forest to hunting and fire.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 compound decline, A1 271. (b) A1 ≈ 34 years (accept rule of 70: 35). (c) R1 R1 valid reasons.

(a) Calculate the total core area for each option. (b) With reference to the SLOSS debate, discuss which design is preferable and suggest one feature that would improve either design.
items.answer: (a) one large: (12 − 2)² = 100 km² (69%); four small: 4 × (6 − 2)² = 64 km² (b) the single large reserve keeps more core habitat for interior species and wide-ranging animals and reduces edge effects; several small reserves spread risk (fire, disease), may include more habitat types and can be easier to acquire; corridors or buffer zones (e.g. UNESCO biosphere reserve model) improve either design.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 100, A1 64. (b) R1 large: edge/area ratio, R1 small: risk-spreading/heterogeneity, R1 corridor/buffer/shape.

items.stem: Which type of species is the grey wolf in Yellowstone, because its removal or return changes the whole ecosystem?
options: A pioneer species
An endemic plant
A keystone species
An invasive species
items.answer: A keystone species
items.markingKey: C. Keystone species have a disproportionate effect relative to abundance.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The IUCN category for a species with inadequate information to assess its extinction risk"?
options: Critically Endangered
Endangered
Data Deficient
edge effect
items.answer: Data Deficient
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Data Deficient.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Rewilding means abandoning land and doing nothing." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rewilding often involves active steps - reintroducing species, removing drainage or fences - before stepping back to let processes operate.
items.markingKey: Rewilding often involves active steps - reintroducing species, removing drainage or fences - before stepping back to let processes operate. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Chloé writes: "All non-native species are invasive." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most introduced species do not become invasive; only those that spread and cause harm are called invasive (e.g. many crop plants are non-native but not invasive).
items.markingKey: Most introduced species do not become invasive; only those that spread and cause harm are called invasive (e.g. many crop plants are non-native but not invasive). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State two differences between in situ conservation and ex situ conservation.
items.answer: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat with their ecological interactions; ex situ conservation keeps them outside it (zoos, seed banks) as a back-up or for captive breeding.
items.markingKey: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat with their ecological interactions; ex situ conservation keeps them outside it (zoos, seed banks) as a back-up or for captive breeding. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Briefly explain why the IUCN Red List is useful for conservation.
items.answer: It uses objective, standard criteria to rank extinction risk, identifies priorities, informs legislation (e.g. CITES, national laws), monitors trends over time (Red List Index) and raises public awareness.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It uses objective, standard criteria to rank extinction risk, identifies priorities, informs legislation (e.g. CITES, national laws), monitors trends over time (Red List Index) and raises public awareness. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Convention on Biological Diversity and CITES.
items.answer: CITES regulates international trade in listed species; the CBD is a broader treaty on conserving all biodiversity, sustainable use and benefit sharing, with targets such as the Kunming-Montreal framework.
items.markingKey: CITES regulates international trade in listed species; the CBD is a broader treaty on conserving all biodiversity, sustainable use and benefit sharing, with targets such as the Kunming-Montreal framework. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity even when the total area of habitat lost is small.
items.answer: Small patches support smaller populations (more vulnerable to inbreeding and chance events), edge effects reduce interior habitat, and isolation prevents dispersal and recolonisation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the kākāpō recovery programme, New Zealand shows species-based conservation.
items.answer: By moving all birds to predator-free islands and intensive management, numbers rose from 51 in 1995 to about 250 by 2024. Intensive, single-species management removed predation and boosted breeding of a flightless parrot.

items.answer: With no breeding males the population cannot recover naturally, showing the cost of acting too late.

items.stem: Outline how beaver reintroduction can benefit biodiversity and reduce flood risk.
items.answer: Beaver dams create wetlands and ponds that store water, slow peak flows and reduce downstream flooding, trap sediment and create habitat for amphibians, invertebrates and fish (e.g. Devon beaver trial).
